book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 7

clue.text: Hating union, Sammy and I go off

indicators.note: Milk goes off when it will no longer keep, and letters that have gone off no longer keep the order they were handed over in.

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters; 'and' is only the join

explanation.surface: Sammy and I walk out in disgust at the union.
explanation.walkthrough: Union here is marriage, not the trade sort, and the word wanted names hatred of the institution itself. Its better-known cousin misogyny is hatred of women.
explanation.definitionFit: Misogamy is the hatred of marriage, and a union is a marriage — the definition reads as the hating of union.

clue.text: Girl, one with a title in G. & S.

indicators.note: In puts one thing inside another, so the titled woman goes between the two initials rather than in front of them.

parts.note: G and S are Gilbert and Sullivan, the Victorian pair behind the Savoy operas, and their initials part to take a filling
a lady holds her title in her own right or by marriage

explanation.surface: A girl with a title of her own, somewhere in Gilbert and Sullivan.
explanation.walkthrough: G. & S. is Gilbert and Sullivan, whose comic operas really are full of titled ladies. The initials are not pointing at a character, though — they are two letters to write down with the peerage in between.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladys is an ordinary girl's given name, so the definition names the answer by the kind of thing it is.

clue.text: Turned aside, deserted, left locked in

indicators.note: Something locked in is shut up inside something else, so the letter beside it is held within the word just named.

parts.note: a soldier who deserted his own side defected to the other one
L is the standard short form for left

explanation.surface: An abandoned building: passed by, emptied out and shut up.
explanation.walkthrough: Three past participles in a row read as one abandoned building, so the commas look like nothing but a list. 'Left' is not part of that picture — it is the single letter L.
explanation.definitionFit: A ball or a question that has been deflected was turned aside from the line it was travelling on.

clue.text: One making rapid progress round western peninsula

indicators.note: Round means encircling, so the piece named before it closes about the letter that follows.

parts.note: a goer is someone who gets on with it at speed
W is the compass point west

explanation.surface: A fast mover travelling round a peninsula in the west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Western' reads as part of the description of the peninsula, which is exactly why it is easy to miss as wordplay. The name also belongs to David Gower, England's left-handed batsman of the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Gower is a peninsula of south Wales, reaching west from Swansea into the Bristol Channel — a place name doing duty as the definition.

clue.text: Vulgar tattler that everyone's talking about

parts.note: calling a person common is calling them vulgar, in the snobbish British sense
a tattler tells tales about other people, which is what a gossip does

explanation.surface: A coarse tell-tale who has himself become the talk of the neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves of the wordplay describe a person and the definition describes a thing — the talk itself, not the talker. Calling somebody vulgar in this particular way is a class insult in Britain rather than a remark about manners.
explanation.definitionFit: News that is common gossip is being passed round by everybody, which is exactly what everyone is talking about.

clue.text: See old actor pine, for instance

definitions.meaning: the stage surname of Sir Herbert Beerbohm, the actor-manager who built His Majesty's Theatre in London and died in 1917
one species standing for the whole kind, which is what 'for instance' admits

explanation.surface: Watching a veteran of the stage yearn for something lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pine' is a verb in the surface and a conifer in the answer, and 'for instance' is the setter admitting he has offered only one species. The actor is Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree, remembered now chiefly by crossword setters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Herbert Beerbohm Tree was a celebrated actor-manager, and a pine is one species of tree — the definition by example that 'for instance' flags.

clue.text: Dressing, including equipment for banditry

indicators.note: To include something is to have it inside you, so the dressing takes the equipment in among its own letters.

parts.note: a bandage is the dressing put on a wound
a rig is the gear or tackle a job calls for

explanation.surface: A wound dressing packed in with the gear a highwayman needs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dressing' is the hospital kind, neither salad nor clothing. The definition is an abstract noun: the practice of robbery, not the men who practise it.
explanation.definitionFit: Brigandage is robbery carried on by armed gangs on the roads, which is what banditry means.

clue.text: Winds up at port almost intact — a narrow escape

indicators.note: What is almost intact is whole but for a piece missing, so the word beside it arrives one letter short.

parts.note: a company that winds up its affairs closes
a port is a haven, docked here of its final letter

explanation.surface: A battered ship reaches harbour with barely a scratch on her.
explanation.walkthrough: The two pieces do not line up with the two words: the join falls a letter past the space, which is what hides it. 'Winds up' is the finishing sort, nothing to do with weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A close shave is a brush with disaster that misses you by a hair, which is a narrow escape.

clue.text: Arguments for ordinary language, not English

indicators.note: Not cancels whatever comes after it, so the letter named there is struck out of the word before.

parts.note: prose is language as it is ordinarily written, set against verse
E is the standard short form for English, and it is the letter dropped

explanation.surface: The case for plain speech instead of formal English.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition needs its preposition: the arguments on the other side would be a different word entirely. 'Not' is doing a crossword's work here, striking a letter out rather than setting two languages against each other.
explanation.definitionFit: The pros are the points put forward in favour of something, the for side of a pros-and-cons list.

clue.text: Essayist is a bachelor engaged in foreign currency study

indicators.note: To be engaged in something is to be caught up inside it, so the words before go within the two pieces that follow.

parts.note: the franc was France's money before the euro
the clue's own word, taken exactly as it stands
a bachelor of arts is a BA
to con a thing is to study it closely, an old sense crosswords keep alive

explanation.surface: An unmarried man taking a course in foreign exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Study' is the verb, not the room, and 'currency study' looks like one subject when it is two separate pieces with the rest driven between them. The essayist was also Lord Chancellor, and was sacked for taking bribes.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon's Essays of 1597 gave English the word essay for a short prose piece, so the definition names him squarely.

clue.text: Money that will obtain some myrrh in Orient

indicators.note: Some asks for a part of what follows rather than the whole of it, and the part wanted runs straight through the words without a break.

parts.note: the letters run unbroken across all three words, starting two letters into the spice and stopping at the first letter of the east

explanation.surface: Cash enough to buy a little myrrh in an eastern market.
explanation.walkthrough: Three short words in a row are where hidden answers like to live, and the gift-of-the-Magi picture keeps the eye on meaning rather than letters: myr|RH IN O|rient. 'In' belongs to the hiding place, not to any instruction to insert.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhino has meant ready cash in English slang since the seventeenth century, and survives in the phrase ready rhino.

clue.text: Unseemly incident after fall brings down curtain

indicators.note: After puts one thing behind another, so the incident is written second and the fall goes in front of it.

parts.note: a fall in temperature or in price is a drop
making a scene in public is causing an unseemly fuss

explanation.surface: An ugly row after somebody's downfall ends the evening's entertainment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brings down' looks like the point of the sentence and is only the join; the definition is the single word at the end. 'Fall' is a plain descent here, not anybody's disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: A drop-scene is the painted cloth lowered at the front of a stage between acts — a curtain in all but name.

clue.text: Jargon of tinkers heard in harbour

indicators.note: Heard asks for the sound of the word rather than its spelling, and 'in' points at the word whose sound is wanted.

parts.note: to harbour someone is to shelter them, and British speech does not sound that final R

explanation.surface: Travellers' slang overheard on the quayside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbour' is the verb, not the dock, and reading the whole clue as a place is the trap. British speech drops the final R, which is the only reason the sound comes out right.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelta is the secret cant of Irish tinkers and travellers, made largely of disguised Irish words — a jargon in the exact sense.

clue.text: Taken aback, initially surprised, then badly rattled

indicators.note: Initially asks for no more of a word than the letter it begins with.
What is done badly comes out wrong, and letters that come out wrong are letters in the wrong order.

parts.note: the opening letter of surprised
anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Someone caught out shows surprise first and is thoroughly shaken after.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taken aback' is the definition, though it reads like an instruction to turn something round — that is the trap. 'Then' is doing nothing but keeping the surface's story in sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: To be startled is to be caught unawares by something sudden, which is what taken aback describes.

clue.text: Demented oriental Peter rendered harmless

parts.note: mad is demented, out of one's wits
the orient is the east, and E is the compass point
in British thieves' slang a peter is a strongbox

explanation.surface: A deranged easterner called Peter is finally neutralised.
explanation.walkthrough: Peter is not a man here — in British thieves' slang it is a strongbox, which is why the men who cracked them were petermen. The answer runs on into 2 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb or a weapon that has been made safe has been rendered harmless, which is the phrase disposal teams use.

clue.text: See 1
Enters the stage and talks at length

definitions.meaning: the actor's cue: to go on is to walk out in front of the audience
and to go on, and on, is to talk past everybody's patience

explanation.surface: An actor takes the stage and then will not stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves describe the same actor, which is why the surface reads as one sentence instead of two definitions. The second sense usually comes doubled in speech — people go on and on.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor goes on when he walks out before the audience, and anyone who goes on is talking far longer than you wanted.

clue.text: Completely changed, home team drops out

indicators.note: Something out of true is not where it should be, and letters not where they should be are letters to be rearranged.

parts.note: anagram fodder, thirteen letters

explanation.surface: The home side is knocked out of the competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drops out' reads as one phrasal verb and the setter has split it, so only the first of the two words supplies letters. The definition wants a change of form rather than of state: a grub into a beetle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something metamorphosed has turned into a different form altogether, which is what completely changed describes.

clue.text: Poultry with hard excrescence in limbs

indicators.note: In puts one thing within another, so the growth sits inside the limbs instead of beside them.

parts.note: legs are the limbs you stand on, and the word opens after three letters
a horn is a hard outgrowth from an animal's head

explanation.surface: Birds carrying a hard growth somewhere about their legs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a diseased bird and the wordplay has nothing to do with poultry at all. 'Hard excrescence' is a deliberately clinical way of naming something an animal grows on its head.
explanation.definitionFit: Leghorns are the white Italian laying hens named after Leghorn, the old English name for the port of Livorno — poultry by breed.

clue.text: Depressed over disturbances involving one on the ground floor?

indicators.note: In a down entry over means directly above, so the piece named first is written at the top and the rest below it.

parts.note: someone low in spirits is down

indicators.note: To involve something is to wrap it up in what you are doing, so the disturbances close round the letter that follows.

parts.note: a stir is a commotion, as in causing quite a stir
a is the indefinite article standing in for one

explanation.surface: Feeling low about the trouble involving somebody on the ground floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' is doing a job peculiar to down clues: it means above on the page, not about. The question mark is the setter conceding that the floor below need not be the ground floor.
explanation.definitionFit: To be downstairs is to be on the floor below the one you are on, which in an ordinary house is the ground floor.

clue.text: Cabaret act tries a step that's novel

indicators.note: Novel means newly made, and letters made new are the same letters standing in a new order.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A cabaret turn attempting a dance step nobody has seen before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' is an adjective here rather than a book, and it is the only word asking for anything to be rearranged. The definition names the turn, not the person performing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A strip-tease is a staged undressing performed as a turn in a club or cabaret, so the definition names it by kind.

clue.text: Refrain from sounding horn — show complete unconcern

definitions.meaning: read word by word: a hoot is the noise a horn makes, and the instruction is not to make it
the idiom as everybody uses it: to care nothing at all

explanation.surface: A notice telling drivers not to sound their horns.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition reads an idiom literally, word by word, while the second takes it as it is meant. The dash marks the join between those two senses rather than a pause in one sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To not give a hoot is to care nothing whatever, and taken literally it is also an instruction to sound no hooter.

clue.text: Ranches store noisy weapons

parts.note: the stock is what a shop keeps in store
f is forte, the musician's direction to play loudly
arms are weapons — to take up arms is to take up weapons

explanation.surface: Ranches keeping a lot of loud firearms in store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noisy' is not describing the weapons: f is the musician's mark for loud, one of the handful of Italian directions crosswords lean on. The join between the last two pieces falls inside the second word, where the hyphen is no help.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock farm is one that raises livestock — stock — which is what a ranch is for.

clue.text: Ornamental bit of embroidery — blimey! — kept in case

indicators.note: What is kept in is held inside something else, so the pieces named before go within the word that follows.

parts.note: the dative is the grammatical case of the indirect object in Latin and German

indicators.note: A bit of a word is a fragment of it, and the fragment wanted first is the letter it begins with.

parts.note: the opening letter of embroidery
cor is a British exclamation of astonishment, as in cor blimey

explanation.surface: A fancy scrap of needlework — good heavens — packed away in a box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' is the grammarian's, not the suitcase, and 'blimey' is in the clue for its shorter cousin rather than for itself. The dashes make the exclamation look like an aside when it is carrying letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Something decorative is there to adorn rather than to work, which is precisely what ornamental means.

clue.text: Stretch forth one's hand, touching a child away from home

parts.note: re means concerning, the sense that survives in touching the matter in hand
the article as it stands, then CH, the standard short form for child
someone away from home is out

explanation.surface: Offering a hand to a child a long way from home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touching' is the letter-writer's word for concerning, not a hand on a shoulder, and it is the first thing the surface wants you to misread. The definition is biblical in tone on purpose.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach out is to extend the arm towards something or someone, which is to stretch forth one's hand.

clue.text: Coin-spinner or angry bull?

definitions.note: A tosser is anyone or anything that tosses; an angry bull is an example rather than a synonym, which is what the question mark concedes.
definitions.meaning: the man who flips the coin before the match starts
a bull throws what it catches on its horns, so it earns the same agent noun

explanation.surface: Is it the man flipping the coin, or the bull in the field?
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings hang on the same verb, and the question mark marks the second as an example rather than a definition proper. In British slang the word is also an insult, which the setter quietly leaves alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Whoever spins the coin tosses it, and a bull that throws a man on its horns tosses him too — one agent noun covers both.

clue.text: Erudite and fit cardinal, we hear?

parts.note: someone in good health

indicators.note: We hear asks for the sound of the word meant, so what gets written down is spelt differently from what you would say.

parts.note: cardinal is a deep red, the colour of a cardinal's robes, and the past tense of the verb is said the same way

explanation.surface: A learned churchman who is in good health too, by all accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' is the colour, not the churchman: the scarlet robes gave the shade its name. The answer runs across two entries, 22 and 23 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone well-read has got their learning out of books, which is what erudite describes.

clue.text: See 22
